patient.name: Priya Raman
patient.complaint: Constant right upper quadrant pain and fever for 2 days
background: Episodes of RUQ pain after takeaways over the past year

diagnosis.exam: Expect 'Which is the most likely diagnosis?' with constant RUQ pain, fever and a positive Murphy's sign in a woman with the 4 F's, and 'most likely organism' (E. coli) or 'most likely complication' questions.

points: Priya, 46, has **constant RUQ pain** for 2 days.
It started after a fatty takeaway and has not settled.
Pain spreads to her **right shoulder blade**.
She feels hot and has vomited twice.

steps.lead: Priya's past biliary colic tells you she has stones; now one is stuck in the **cystic duct** and the gallbladder is inflamed.
Priya fits the **4 F's**: female, fat (BMI 34), forty-something and fertile (three children).

visual.title: Where Priya's pain is
visual.caption: Right upper quadrant pain radiating to the right shoulder or scapula: referred via the diaphragm.

steps.lead: Priya has the classic triad of **RUQ pain, fever and vomiting** after a fatty meal; **E. coli** is the likely organism.

points: Pressing the RUQ, she **stops breathing in** sharply.
The same test on the left is painless.

steps.lead: Priya has a **positive Murphy's sign**: inspiratory arrest on the right, negative on the left.

steps.title: Biliary colic vs cholecystitis vs cholangitis
head: Feature
Biliary colic
Acute cholecystitis
Ascending cholangitis

steps.q: Which feature most clearly tells you Priya has cholecystitis rather than biliary colic?
steps.r: **Inflammation** (fever, Murphy's, raised markers) separates cholecystitis from colic. Meal trigger, radiation and vomiting occur in both.

steps.lead: If Priya were left untreated, the gallbladder could **perforate** or fill with pus (**empyema**).
After Priya's operation, bile in her drain with abnormal LFTs would mean a **bile leak**, managed with **ERCP**.

steps.text: Jaundice is **not** a feature of simple cholecystitis. RUQ pain + fever + **jaundice** = ascending cholangitis (stone in the CBD).

investigation.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?' where the answer is abdominal ultrasound, and 'most likely finding' questions on the scan (wall thickening, pericholecystic fluid) or bloods (raised CRP and WCC).

steps.q: Which test should Priya have first to confirm the diagnosis?
steps.r: **Ultrasound** is first-line: it shows the stones and the inflamed gallbladder, with no radiation.

steps.lead: Priya's scan shows **gallstones**, a **thickened gallbladder wall** (6 mm) and **pericholecystic fluid**, plus a sonographic Murphy's sign.

steps.title: Priya's bloods
steps.text: Inflammation without jaundice; normal amylase excludes pancreatitis.

steps.lead: Priya's **CRP 148 and WCC 16.2** confirm inflammation; mildly abnormal LFTs are common.

visual.title: Gallbladder wall thickness on ultrasound
visual.label: Priya 6 mm
visual.caption: A wall over 3 mm, with stones and pericholecystic fluid, supports acute cholecystitis.

steps.text: Do not pick CT or MRCP first. **Ultrasound** is first-line; MRCP is for suspected stones in the **common bile duct**.
Normal bilirubin and an undilated CBD mean no duct stone, so **no ERCP**. Check amylase to exclude gallstone pancreatitis.

management.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate initial management?' (IV fluids, analgesia, IV antibiotics) and questions on the penicillin-allergic regimen and timing of laparoscopic cholecystectomy (within 1 week).

steps.q: Priya is penicillin allergic. Which antibiotics should she get?
steps.r: Co-amoxiclav is first-line, but she is **penicillin allergic**: **cefuroxime + metronidazole**. Tazocin contains a penicillin.

steps.lead: Priya gets **IV fluids, analgesia** and **IV cefuroxime plus metronidazole** because of her allergy.

steps.title: Acute cholecystitis pathway
nodes: Early laparoscopic cholecystectomy (≤72 h, within 1 week)
Unfit or empyema worsening → percutaneous cholecystostomy
steps.caption: Treat the infection, then remove the gallbladder early.

visual.title: Timing of cholecystectomy from onset
visual.label: Priya day 2.5
visual.caption: Priya is listed on day 2, inside the 72-hour ideal window.

steps.lead: Priya has an **early laparoscopic cholecystectomy** this admission, which stops future attacks.

visual.title: Priya's response to treatment
visual.caption: Fever and CRP fall with antibiotics and source removal. A rising CRP despite antibiotics would suggest empyema.

steps.lead: Priya's plan follows **NICE gallstone guidance** and the **Tokyo Guidelines**: antibiotics, then early surgery within a week.

steps.text: Do not send her home to wait 6 weeks for an 'interval' operation. Early cholecystectomy (**within 1 week**) is the standard.

science.exam: Expect applied questions: why a blocked cystic duct inflames the gallbladder, which organism infects it (E. coli), why Murphy's sign is positive, and why it can progress to empyema or perforation.

steps.lead: Priya's stone blocked the **cystic duct**, so the gallbladder could not empty: bile stagnated and the wall became inflamed and distended.

steps.title: From stone to sepsis
nodes: Gallstone impacts in the cystic duct
Secondary infection with gut bacteria (E. coli)

steps.lead: The bacteria in Priya's gallbladder are enteric, most often **E. coli**, which drives her fever, CRP and WCC.

steps.q: Which organism most likely infected Priya's gallbladder?
steps.r: **E. coli** (an enteric Gram-negative rod) is the commonest; Klebsiella and Enterococcus also occur.

steps.lead: Had Priya's obstruction persisted, wall **ischaemia** could have led to gangrene, **empyema** or **perforation**.
When Priya breathes in, the diaphragm pushes her inflamed gallbladder onto the examiner's hand, irritating the peritoneum: **Murphy's sign**.

steps.text: The **left-sided** check matters: generalised peritonitis hurts on both sides, so Murphy's sign is only specific when the left is negative.

o: Cystic duct obstruction by a gallstone
mcq.r: A gallstone blocks the **cystic duct**; a CBD stone gives cholangitis.

mcq.q: Which sign is classically positive in cholecystitis?
mcq.r: **Murphy's sign**: inspiratory arrest on RUQ palpation.

mcq.q: What is the most likely causative organism?
Gallbladder empyema is worsening despite antibiotics. What is needed?
What is the first-line investigation for suspected cholecystitis?

mcq.r: **Raised CRP and WCC**, often with abnormal LFTs.

mcq.q: What is first-line antibiotic therapy (no allergy)?
mcq.r: **Co-amoxiclav** IV; cefuroxime + metronidazole if penicillin allergic.

mcq.q: When should laparoscopic cholecystectomy be done?
How is a post-cholecystectomy bile leak managed?
mcq.r: **ERCP** (usually with a stent) lets bile drain into the duodenum.

o: Inflamed gallbladder pushed onto the hand during inspiration
mcq.r: Diaphragmatic descent pushes the **inflamed gallbladder** against the hand, irritating the peritoneum.

technique.stem: A 43 year old woman has a 2 day history of constant right upper quadrant pain radiating to her right shoulder, with nausea and vomiting. It began after a fatty meal. Her temperature is 38.3°C, pulse rate 102 bpm and BP 126/80 mmHg. She is not jaundiced. On palpation of the right upper quadrant she stops breathing in.
technique.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

steps.x: A diagnosis question about RUQ pain: decide colic vs cholecystitis vs cholangitis.
Constant pain + fever = inflammation; positive **Murphy's sign**; no jaundice.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: Amylase is normal and pain is not epigastric to the back.
Cholangitis needs jaundice; bilirubin is normal.
Colic has no fever and normal inflammatory markers.
No cough, breathlessness or chest signs; Murphy's sign points to the gallbladder.

steps.x: **A. Acute cholecystitis.** RUQ pain + fever + Murphy's, no jaundice.

technique.stem: A 50 year old woman has a 24 hour history of constant right upper quadrant pain and fever. Her temperature is 38.0°C, pulse rate 98 bpm and BP 132/84 mmHg. Murphy's sign is positive. She is not jaundiced.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?

steps.x: Initial investigation: the first imaging test for the likely diagnosis.

clues: constant right upper quadrant pain and fever
steps.x: Acute cholecystitis; no sign of a duct stone.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: Most gallstones are not visible on X-ray.
CT is not first-line and misses many stones.
ERCP is treatment for duct stones, not a first test.
MRCP is for suspected CBD stones when ultrasound is unclear.

steps.x: **A. Abdominal ultrasound.** Shows stones, thick wall and pericholecystic fluid.

technique.stem: A 38 year old woman has acute cholecystitis confirmed on ultrasound. She has a history of anaphylaxis to penicillin. Her temperature is 38.5°C, pulse rate 106 bpm and BP 118/74 mmHg. She has been given IV fluids and analgesia.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate antibiotic treatment?

steps.x: Antibiotic choice: check the allergy status first.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Usual first-line is co-amoxiclav; with penicillin allergy, **cefuroxime + metronidazole**.

elim: Amoxicillin is a penicillin.
Co-amoxiclav contains amoxicillin.
Piperacillin is a penicillin.
Nitrofurantoin is for urinary infection only.

steps.x: **B. IV cefuroxime and metronidazole.** The notes' penicillin-allergic regimen.

technique.stem: A 47 year old woman has acute cholecystitis. Her temperature is 38.6°C, pulse rate 104 bpm and BP 122/76 mmHg. Blood cultures grow a Gram-negative rod that ferments lactose.
technique.q: Which is the most likely causative organism?

steps.x: An organism question: think of where the bacteria come from.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Secondary infection by gut flora: **E. coli**.

elim: C. difficile is a Gram-positive cause of colitis.
Pseudomonas does not ferment lactose.
S. aureus is a Gram-positive coccus.
S. pyogenes is a Gram-positive coccus.

steps.x: **B. Escherichia coli.** Cholecystitis organism = enteric, most often E. coli.

practice.stem: A 41 year old woman has a 3 day history of constant right upper quadrant pain radiating to her right scapula, with nausea and vomiting. She has three children and a BMI of 36. Her temperature is 38.2°C, pulse rate 100 bpm and BP 130/82 mmHg. The right upper quadrant is tender with guarding. She is not jaundiced.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Constant RUQ pain with fever and raised inflammatory markers but normal bilirubin is acute cholecystitis. Biliary colic has no fever and normal bloods; cholangitis has jaundice.

steps.x: Diagnosis: place her on the colic, cholecystitis, cholangitis ladder.

clues: 3 day history of constant right upper quadrant pain
three children and a BMI of 36
steps.x: 4 F's, constant pain over 6 hours, fever, no jaundice.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: Amylase is normal.
No jaundice; bilirubin normal.
Colic settles within hours, without fever.
Ulcer pain is epigastric and does not cause fever and guarding like this.

practice.stem: A 52 year old woman has constant right upper quadrant pain and a fever for 1 day. Her temperature is 38.1°C, pulse rate 96 bpm and BP 134/80 mmHg. She is not jaundiced. The site of her pain is shown (see item resources).
practice.q: Which is the most likely finding on examination?
practice.e: Acute cholecystitis gives a positive Murphy's sign: inspiratory arrest on RUQ pressure, negative on the left. A painless palpable gallbladder is Courvoisier's sign of malignancy.

steps.x: A finding question: first name the diagnosis, then its sign.

clues: constant right upper quadrant pain and a fever

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: Periumbilical bruising: haemorrhagic pancreatitis.
Flank bruising: haemorrhagic pancreatitis.
Courvoisier: painless jaundice from malignancy.
Rovsing's sign is for appendicitis.

practice.stem: A 44 year old woman with known gallstones has 2 days of constant right upper quadrant pain, fever and vomiting. Her temperature is 38.7°C, pulse rate 108 bpm and BP 124/76 mmHg. Ultrasound shows a thick-walled gallbladder with stones. Blood cultures are taken.
practice.q: Which is the most likely causative organism?
practice.e: Acute cholecystitis is a secondary infection by enteric organisms, most commonly E. coli. Bacteroides can be present but is less common.

steps.x: Organism question: name the diagnosis, then its commonest bug.

clues: constant right upper quadrant pain, fever and vomiting

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: An anaerobe that can co-infect, but not the commonest.
H. pylori causes gastritis and ulcers.
S. aureus causes skin and bone infection.
Pneumococcus causes pneumonia and meningitis.

practice.stem: A 58 year old man has been treated for 4 days with IV antibiotics for acute cholecystitis. He has swinging fevers and worsening right upper quadrant pain. His temperature is 39.4°C, pulse rate 118 bpm and BP 106/64 mmHg. There is a tender palpable right upper quadrant mass.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Deterioration despite antibiotics with swinging fevers and a tender RUQ mass is gallbladder empyema, needing urgent percutaneous cholecystostomy or surgical drainage.

steps.x: Diagnosis of a complication of treated cholecystitis.

clues: tender palpable right upper quadrant mass
steps.x: Failing antibiotics + swinging fever + mass = pus in the gallbladder.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: Bilirubin is barely raised; cholangitis gives jaundice.
Colic has no fever or mass.
Gallstone ileus is bowel obstruction with pneumobilia.
Mirizzi causes obstructive jaundice from extrinsic duct compression.

practice.stem: A 49 year old woman had a laparoscopic cholecystectomy for acute cholecystitis 2 days ago. She now has increasing abdominal pain and a fever. Her temperature is 38.2°C, pulse rate 104 bpm and BP 120/74 mmHg. Her surgical drain contains green fluid.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Bile in the drain with abnormal LFTs after cholecystectomy is a bile leak, from a slipped cystic duct clip or duct injury, and is managed with ERCP.

steps.x: A post-operative diagnosis: look at the drain.
Bile in the drain after gallbladder surgery.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: Ileus gives distension and no bowel sounds, not bile in a drain.
The gallbladder has been removed.
Perforation gives faeculent or enteric contents and peritonism.
Wound infection does not put bile in the drain.

practice.stem: A 45 year old woman has acute cholecystitis. Her temperature is 38.0°C, pulse rate 98 bpm and BP 128/82 mmHg. A medical student asks what has started the inflammation.
practice.q: Which is the most likely underlying cause?
practice.e: Acute cholecystitis is caused by a gallstone obstructing the cystic duct, causing bile stasis and inflammation, then secondary infection.

steps.x: A cause question: what blocks the gallbladder?

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: Alcohol causes pancreatitis and liver disease.
A CBD stricture causes jaundice, not gallbladder inflammation.
Hepatitis B inflames the liver.
Pancreatic tumours cause painless obstructive jaundice.

practice.stem: A 39 year old woman has constant right upper quadrant pain for 18 hours with a temperature of 37.9°C, pulse rate 94 bpm and BP 122/78 mmHg. Murphy's sign is positive and she is not jaundiced.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?
practice.e: Abdominal ultrasound is first-line for suspected cholecystitis. MRCP and ERCP are for common bile duct stones; CT is not first-line.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: Most stones are radiolucent.
CT is second-line and misses stones.
ERCP is therapeutic for duct stones.
HIDA is used only when ultrasound is equivocal.

practice.stem: A 47 year old woman has a 2 day history of constant right upper quadrant pain, fever and vomiting. Her temperature is 38.4°C, pulse rate 102 bpm and BP 130/80 mmHg. Murphy's sign is positive. An abdominal ultrasound is performed.
practice.q: Which is the most likely finding on ultrasound?
o: Dilated common bile duct with a distal stone
Gallstones with gallbladder wall thickening and pericholecystic fluid
practice.e: Acute cholecystitis on ultrasound shows gallstones, a thickened gallbladder wall and pericholecystic fluid. A dilated CBD suggests choledocholithiasis.

steps.x: A finding question: what does cholecystitis look like on the scan?

clues: constant right upper quadrant pain, fever and vomiting

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: A CBD stone is choledocholithiasis; she is not jaundiced.
Double duct sign suggests pancreatic head cancer.
Pneumobilia suggests gallstone ileus or previous sphincterotomy.
Cholecystitis is almost always calculous.

practice.stem: A 42 year old woman has acute cholecystitis confirmed on ultrasound. She has no allergies. Her temperature is 38.3°C, pulse rate 104 bpm and BP 118/72 mmHg. She is in pain and vomiting.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
o: IV fluids, analgesia and IV co-amoxiclav
practice.e: Initial management is IV fluids, analgesia and IV antibiotics (co-amoxiclav), followed by early laparoscopic cholecystectomy. ERCP is for CBD stones.

steps.x: Initial management of an infected gallbladder.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: Surgery should be early, within 1 week.
Discharge is for biliary colic, not infection.
No duct stone or jaundice.
Dissolution therapy has no role in acute infection.

practice.stem: A 40 year old woman has acute cholecystitis and is improving on IV antibiotics after 24 hours. She is otherwise fit and well. Her temperature is 37.6°C, pulse rate 88 bpm and BP 124/78 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate definitive management?
practice.e: Early laparoscopic cholecystectomy, ideally within 72 hours and within 1 week, is definitive and prevents recurrence. Cholecystostomy is for patients unfit for surgery.

steps.x: Fit for surgery, early in the episode.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: High recurrence risk.
No duct stone.
Delayed surgery is not the standard; early is preferred.
For patients unfit for surgery or with worsening empyema.

practice.stem: An 86 year old man with severe heart failure and COPD has acute cholecystitis. Despite 3 days of IV antibiotics he has swinging fevers and a tender right upper quadrant mass. His temperature is 39.1°C, pulse rate 116 bpm and BP 98/60 mmHg. The anaesthetist judges him unfit for surgery.
practice.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
practice.e: A gallbladder empyema deteriorating despite antibiotics in a patient unfit for surgery needs urgent percutaneous cholecystostomy to drain it.

steps.x: Next step in a failing, high-risk patient.
Empyema, failing antibiotics, unfit for operation.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: He is septic and worsening.
ERCP drains the CBD, not the gallbladder.
He is unfit for surgery.
Delay risks perforation.

steps.x: **D.** Drain the pus when surgery is not possible.

practice.stem: A 46 year old woman has acute cholecystitis. Her temperature is 38.2°C, pulse rate 100 bpm and BP 126/80 mmHg. When the right upper quadrant is pressed and she breathes in deeply, she suddenly stops inspiring. The same manoeuvre on the left causes no pain.
practice.q: Which is the most likely explanation for this sign?
o: Compression of the right phrenic nerve
Inflamed gallbladder descending onto the examining hand
Spasm of the sphincter of Oddi
practice.e: Murphy's sign: the diaphragm pushes the inflamed gallbladder down onto the examiner's hand, irritating the overlying peritoneum and halting inspiration.

clues: on the left causes no pain
steps.x: Positive Murphy's sign, specific because the left is negative.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Inspiration pushes the inflamed gallbladder onto the hand.**

elim: Bile peritonitis is generalised, not focal and inspiratory.
Phrenic irritation explains shoulder pain, not the sign.
Capsular stretch causes dull hepatic ache.
Sphincter spasm causes colic, not inspiratory arrest.

steps.x: **D.** Local peritoneal irritation over the inflamed gallbladder.

prompts.q: What is acute cholecystitis, what causes it and who gets it?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: stone in which duct, and the risk profile in the stem.

points.p: Inflammation of the gallbladder
Gallstone obstructing the cystic duct
4 F's: female, fat, forty, fertile

prompts.q: Describe the classic presentation and signature sign of acute cholecystitis.
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: pain, fever and one sign.

points.p: RUQ pain radiating to the right shoulder/scapula
Fever, nausea and vomiting
Worse after fatty meals
Positive Murphy's sign: inspiratory arrest on RUQ pressure, negative on the left
points.why: Must be negative on the left to be specific.

prompts.q: Which features separate cholecystitis from biliary colic and from ascending cholangitis?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: fever and jaundice are the switches.

points.p: Colic: no fever, normal bloods, pain settles within hours
Cholecystitis: fever, raised CRP/WCC, Murphy's positive, no jaundice
Cholangitis: jaundice, fever and RUQ pain (Charcot's triad)

prompts.q: What are the complications of cholecystitis and its surgery, and how is each recognised?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: deterioration despite antibiotics, or bile in a drain.

points.p: Perforation, empyema, sepsis, peritonitis
Empyema worsening on antibiotics: percutaneous cholecystostomy or surgical drainage
points.why: Swinging fevers and a RUQ mass.

points.p: Bile leak: bile in drain, abnormal LFTs; managed with ERCP
points.why: Slipped clip, missed CBD stone or duct injury.

points.p: Post-cholecystectomy syndrome: colicky pain, diarrhoea, new jaundice

prompts.q: What is the first-line investigation for cholecystitis and what does it show? What do the bloods show?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: ultrasound first, bloods support.

points.p: Abdominal ultrasound first-line
Gallstones, wall thickening, pericholecystic fluid
Raised CRP and WCC, abnormal LFTs

prompts.q: What is the initial management of acute cholecystitis, including antibiotics and penicillin allergy?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: always check the allergy line in the stem.

points.p: IV fluids and analgesia
IV co-amoxiclav
Cefuroxime plus metronidazole if penicillin allergic
points.why: Avoid amoxicillin and Tazocin in allergy.

prompts.q: What is the definitive treatment, when is it done, and what if the patient is unfit?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: early, not interval surgery.

points.p: Laparoscopic cholecystectomy
Early: ideally within 72 hours, within 1 week
Unfit for surgery or failing empyema: percutaneous cholecystostomy

prompts.q: Explain the pathophysiology of cholecystitis, from stone to infection to perforation.
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: obstruction, stasis, inflammation, infection, ischaemia.

points.p: Cystic duct obstruction prevents gallbladder emptying
Bile stasis, mucosal inflammation, wall distension
Secondary infection, commonly E. coli
Untreated: wall ischaemia, gangrene, perforation or empyema

prompts.q: Why is Murphy's sign positive in cholecystitis?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: what moves during inspiration?

points.p: Peritoneal irritation over the inflamed gallbladder
Diaphragm descends on inspiration, pushing the gallbladder onto the hand
points.why: Hence the sudden halt in breathing in.

glossary.cholecystitis: Inflammation of the gallbladder, usually from a gallstone blocking the cystic duct.
glossary.cystic duct: The duct draining the gallbladder into the common bile duct.
glossary.common bile duct: The duct carrying bile from the liver and gallbladder to the duodenum.
glossary.gallstones: Hard deposits of cholesterol or pigment formed in the gallbladder.
glossary.biliary colic: Pain from a stone temporarily blocking the cystic duct, without infection.
glossary.Murphy's sign: Sudden halt in breathing in when the RUQ is pressed, from an inflamed gallbladder.
glossary.4 F's: Classic gallstone risk profile: female, fat, forty and fertile.
glossary.RUQ: Right upper quadrant of the abdomen.
glossary.pericholecystic fluid: Fluid around the gallbladder on ultrasound, a sign of inflammation.
glossary.E. coli: Escherichia coli, an enteric Gram-negative rod; the commonest cause of gallbladder infection.
glossary.Escherichia coli: A Gram-negative gut bacterium; the most likely organism in cholecystitis.
glossary.enteric: Relating to the intestine, as in gut bacteria.
glossary.empyema: A collection of pus within a body cavity, here the gallbladder.
glossary.gangrene: Death of tissue from loss of blood supply.
glossary.perforation: A hole through the wall of an organ, spilling its contents.
glossary.peritonitis: Inflammation of the peritoneum, the lining of the abdominal cavity.
glossary.peritonism: Signs of peritoneal irritation: guarding, rebound and rigidity.
glossary.percutaneous cholecystostomy: A drain placed through the skin into the gallbladder, used when surgery is unsafe.
glossary.laparoscopic cholecystectomy: Keyhole surgical removal of the gallbladder.
glossary.bile leak: Bile escaping after gallbladder surgery, e.g. from a slipped cystic duct clip.
glossary.post-cholecystectomy syndrome: Ongoing abdominal pain, diarrhoea or jaundice after gallbladder removal.
glossary.ERCP: Endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography: an endoscopic procedure to image and treat the bile ducts.
glossary.co-amoxiclav: Amoxicillin with clavulanic acid; first-line for cholecystitis, avoid in penicillin allergy.
glossary.cefuroxime: A second-generation cephalosporin antibiotic used with metronidazole in penicillin allergy.
glossary.ascending cholangitis: Infection of the bile ducts from obstruction, with fever, jaundice and RUQ pain.
glossary.Charcot's triad: Fever, jaundice and RUQ pain: ascending cholangitis.
glossary.Tokyo Guidelines: International guidelines for diagnosing and grading acute cholecystitis and cholangitis.
glossary.CRP: C-reactive protein, a blood marker of inflammation.
glossary.WCC: White cell count; raised in infection.
glossary.LFTs: Liver function tests, including bilirubin, ALP, ALT and γGT.
glossary.Courvoisier's sign: Painless palpable gallbladder with jaundice, suggesting malignancy not stones.
glossary.MRCP: MRI scan of the bile and pancreatic ducts, used for suspected duct stones.
